verdict: Avoid new chemical, dye and intermediate exposure in Dahej until the power and safety issues settle; lend only to established, diversified borrowers with proven pass-through and no single-plant dependence.
title: Dahej Chemicals, Dyes & Intermediates: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business is and where cash sits
**Dahej is a gas-fed chemical cluster: naphtha and gas go in, dyes, intermediates, aromatics and speciality chemicals come out, and cash is made or lost on the spread between feedstock cost and product price.** The plant is capital-heavy and the working-capital cycle is long because inventory and receivables sit for months; rating reports flag elevated working-capital intensity that blocks capital in high-growth phases [9]. So when a proposal lands, check the feedstock contract and the customer concentration before you look at the P&L; if the borrower cannot show a pass-through clause, ask for the last four quarters of gross margin by product.

## What has changed now
**The national picture is weak: chemical output fell 0.5% YoY and 1.2% Apr-to-date [D], while bank credit to the sector grew 20.7% YoY [D] — a 21.9 pp gap that means lenders are funding inventory, not demand.** Brent at $113/bbl [D] sits above the $75–100 band, so feedstock and power costs are elevated. Locally, a power struggle has jolted Dahej [2], and past incidents include a boiler blast with eight deaths and a ₹25 crore NGT penalty, plus a pollution-board shutdown order on an SRF plant [3]. **These are local news items, some undated in the feed, so treat them as context, not current fact.**

## Where the growth is
**Peer results show the split: Aarti Industries grew Q2 FY27 revenue 75% to ₹3,668 crore with PAT up 58.5% on 30% volume growth and export demand [5][6], while Gem Aromatics' Dahej ramp-up pushed its consolidated loss to ₹7 crore even as revenue rose 16.2% [1].** Pursue established, diversified speciality players with export contracts and proven pass-through; avoid single-plant ramp-ups where depreciation (₹9.5 crore vs ₹3.1 crore) and finance costs (₹4.7 crore vs ₹3.5 crore) outrun EBITDA [1].

## How to grow safely
**Structure term debt to the commissioning curve, not the peak, and take monthly stock and receivable statements plus a quarterly feedstock-cost reconciliation.** For ramp-up borrowers, require a DSRA of at least one quarter's interest and a covenant that EBITDA margin stays above 7.6% [1]. Collect from customer the power-supply contract and the pollution-board consent status before disbursal.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for margin compression without a matching price increase, inventory days stretching beyond the sector norm, and any regulatory notice.** If a borrower's EBITDA margin falls below the prior-year level while revenue grows, ask for the product-wise price list and the customer-wise ageing.
## What I want from you this month

- Pull the power-supply and consent status for every Dahej chemical exposure (monthly).
- Get product-wise gross margin for the last four quarters from each borrower (quarterly).
- Flag any borrower where finance cost grows faster than EBITDA (quarterly).
watch: Any shutdown notice or supply cut -> freeze new limits and review the account
Margin falls below prior year while revenue grows -> ask for price list and customer ageing
Inventory days stretch beyond sector norm -> reduce limit and seek stock statement
Finance cost grows faster than EBITDA -> require promoter support or DSRA top-up
